steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper examining whether context-based rumor detection models trained and evaluated on static datasets with random splits really generalize to unseen rumors. Define the task, explain the problem with current evaluation, state the research question, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- False rumors and computational detection
- Task definitions: rumor detection vs. rumor verification
- Current two-step approach and the problem with random splits on static datasets
- Contextual information and the open question
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- False rumors
  - claims/stories meant to deceive or mislead; spread faster via social media; harm and confusion (cite)
  - large volume, high velocity -> computational approaches (e.g. supervised rumor detection models) for early detection and analysis (cite)
- Definitions
  - rumor detection: check-worthy unverified claims (rumors) vs. other posts (non-rumors) (cite)
  - rumor verification: True, False, Unverified, or Non-Rumor (cite)
- Current approach
  - (i) features from textual content (e.g. source post) + contextual information
  - (ii) train/evaluate on static datasets with random splits (cite)
  - previous studies (cite): random-split evaluation may not reflect generalizability to unseen rumors
  - but those studies only standard text classifiers (e.g. logistic regression), source-post features only
- Context
  - rumors come with comments, user profile features, images
  - Figure 1: two Weibo users post same rumor about death of a famous Chinese actor; same source post, different comments and profile attributes
  - most current models rely on context-based features + random splits (cite)
  - question: do context-based models trained with random splits also overestimate?
  - focus: systematic evaluation of actual generalization (detecting rumors not previously known); hitherto unstudied
- Four contributions
  - empirical proof (§ 4.1 & 5): models struggle with unseen future rumors, some worse than random baselines (Table 3)
  - ablation (§ 5.3) removing source posts: over-reliance on source post, context neglected
  - similarity analysis (§ 5.4) on content and context features: effect of split strategies
  - practical recommendations (§ 6): extra cleaning of static datasets, better evaluation metrics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
False rumors are claims or stories that are meant to deceive or mislead the public, and they can spread faster through social media, which causes harm and confusion. Because there are so many of them and they spread so fast, computational approaches (e.g., supervised rumor detection models) are usually used to detect and analyze false rumors early.

The task of rumor detection usually means distinguishing check-worthy unverified claims (i.e., rumors) from other kinds of posts in social media (non-rumors). Rumor verification, on the other hand, is usually the task of classifying a rumor as True, False, Unverified, or Non-Rumor.

Current computational rumor detection systems usually use a two-step approach: (i) features are extracted from the textual content of the rumor (e.g., source post) together with contextual information, and then (ii) models are trained and evaluated on static datasets with random data splits.

As demonstrated by previous studies, evaluating rumor detection systems on static datasets with random splits might not give an accurate picture of how well such models generalize to unseen rumors. But the evaluation in those studies only looks at standard text classifiers (like logistic regression) and only uses features from source posts.

- Context
  - rumors come with comments, user profile features, images
  - Figure 1: two Weibo users, same rumor about death of a famous Chinese actor, different comments and profile attributes
  - most current models use context-based features + random splits
  - question: do they also overestimate? systematic evaluation of actual generalization, hitherto unstudied
- Four contributions
  - empirical proof (§ 4.1 & 5), some worse than random baselines (Table 3)
  - ablation (§ 5.3): over-reliance on source post
  - similarity analysis (§ 5.4): effect of split strategies
  - recommendations (§ 6): cleaning static datasets, better evaluation metrics

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
False rumors are claims or stories that are meant to deceive or mislead the public, and they can spread faster through social media, which causes harm and confusion. Because there are so many of them and they spread so fast, computational approaches (e.g., supervised rumor detection models) are usually used to detect and analyze false rumors early.

The task of rumor detection usually means distinguishing check-worthy unverified claims (i.e., rumors) from other kinds of posts in social media (non-rumors). Rumor verification, on the other hand, is usually the task of classifying a rumor as True, False, Unverified, or Non-Rumor.

Current computational rumor detection systems usually use a two-step approach: (i) features are extracted from the textual content of the rumor (e.g., source post) together with contextual information, and then (ii) models are trained and evaluated on static datasets with random data splits.

As demonstrated by previous studies, evaluating rumor detection systems on static datasets with random splits might not give an accurate picture of how well such models generalize to unseen rumors. But the evaluation in those studies only looks at standard text classifiers (like logistic regression) and only uses features from source posts.

Rumors in social media also come with a lot of contextual information, like comments, user profile features and images, which complement the text of the source posts. For example, Figure 1 shows two Weibo users who post the same rumor about the death of a famous Chinese actor. The source posts are identical, but the rest of the contextual information (e.g., comments and user profile attributes) is completely different. Most current rumor detection models are developed using context-based features and random data splits.

So the question is whether rumor detection models trained with contextual information on random data splits also tend to overestimate. This paper therefore mainly focuses on systematically evaluating the actual generalization capabilities (i.e., detecting rumors that are not previously known) of context-based rumor detection models, which is a research question that has not been studied so far.

The four contributions of this work are:

- • Empirical proof (§ 4.1 & 5) that even with additional contextual information, rumor detection models still struggle to detect unseen rumors that appear at a future date, and some models are even worse than random baselines (see Table 3).

- • An ablation study (§ 5.3) removing source posts from the inputs, which showed that current rumor detection approaches rely too much on information from the source post and neglect the contextual information.

- • A follow-up similarity analysis (§ 5.4) on content and context-based features, which explains how training/test split strategies affect model performance.

- • Finally, practical recommendations (§ 6) on using static datasets for rumor detection effectively, such as additional cleaning measures for the static dataset and improving the current evaluation metrics.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
False rumors are claims or stories intended to deceive or mislead the public, and they can spread faster through social media, causing harm and confusion [1,2,3]. Due to their large volume and high velocity of spread, computational approaches (e.g., supervised rumor detection models) are typically employed to detect and analyze false rumors at an early stage [4,5,6].

Specifically, rumor detection typically distinguishes check-worthy unverified claims (i.e., rumors) from other kinds of posts in social media (non-rumors) [2], whereas rumor verification is typically the task of classifying a rumor as True, False, Unverified, or Non-Rumor [7].

Current computational rumor detection systems typically follow a two-step approach: (i) features are extracted from the textual content of the rumor (e.g., source post) along with contextual information, and (ii) models are trained and evaluated on static datasets using random data splits [8,9].

As shown by [10,11], evaluating rumor detection systems on static datasets using random splits might not give an accurate picture of how well such models generalize to unseen rumors. Note that the evaluation by [10,11] focuses solely on standard text classifiers (such as logistic regression) using only features derived from source posts.

However, rumors in social media also come with rich contextual information, including comments, user profile features and images, which complement the text of the source posts. For example, Figure 1 shows two Weibo users posting the same rumor about the death of a famous Chinese actor. Although the source posts are identical, the remaining contextual information (e.g., comments and user profile attributes) is completely different. Note that most current rumor detection models rely on context-based features and are developed using random data splits [4,12].

The question that arises is whether rumor detection models trained with contextual information on random data splits may also tend to overestimate performance. This paper therefore focuses on systematically evaluating the actual generalization capabilities (i.e., detecting rumors that are not previously known) of context-based rumor detection models, a research question that has not been studied so far.

The four contributions of this work are:

- • Empirical proof (§ 4.1 & 5) that despite additional contextual information, rumor detection models still struggle to detect unseen rumors appearing at a future date, with some models performing even worse than random baselines (see Table 3).

- • An ablation study (§ 5.3) removing source posts from the inputs, which revealed that current rumor detection approaches rely excessively on the source post while neglecting the contextual information.

- • A follow-up similarity analysis (§ 5.4) of content and context-based features, which elucidates how training/test split strategies affect model performance.

- • Finally, practical recommendations (§ 6) for effectively using static datasets for rumor detection, such as additional cleaning measures for the static dataset and enhanced evaluation metrics.
